Multistage fine-tuning of Whisper for Marathi, Odia and Kannada

Good morning. We are team IndicBridge: I'm Parth, with Gourab, Divyansh and Kaushal.

The cards behind the title are real sentences from our test sets, in Hindi, Kannada, Odia and Marathi.

Our question fits on one line: when a speech model learns a low-resource language better after first learning a related one, is that because the languages are related, or just because it saw more data?

I'll set up the problem, Gourab explains how we tested it, and Divyansh and Kaushal present the results.

Whisper officially supports 99 languages, Hindi among them. But listen to the middle line: untrained whisper-base heard this Hindi sentence and wrote it in romanized English letters.

After we trained it on 45 hours of Hindi, the bottom line is almost word-perfect.

Untrained, the error rate is above 100% for all four languages: 154.7 for Hindi, 194.2 for Odia. Above 100 means the output is longer than the sentence and mostly wrong.

And Odia, spoken by tens of millions, has no language token in Whisper at all. So "supported" does not mean usable. These languages need adaptation.

IndicBridge
PKParth Khandagale· Introduction

A related language helps first. But why?

Earlier work · Pillai et al., 2026

Tamil first, then Malasar

Whisper adapted to Tamil, then to Malasar (a Dravidian language with about 4.5 hours of data): 51.9% WER, 4.5 points better than training on Malasar alone.

They credit the gain to the two languages being related.

What nobody tested

Two explanations fit

Relatedness: the pivot shares sounds, words and grammar with the target.

Just more data: any extra speech and an extra training stage would have helped as much.

Only an unrelated pivot of the same size can tell them apart.

So we added one.

The idea we build on is multistage fine-tuning. Pillai and colleagues trained Whisper on Tamil first, then on Malasar, a tiny Dravidian language, and got 4.5 points fewer errors than training on Malasar alone.

They explain it by relatedness: Tamil and Malasar are cousins. But there's a second explanation that fits the same result: maybe any extra speech would have helped, related or not.

The only way to tell those apart is a control: an unrelated pivot language, with the same amount of data and the same training. Nobody had run that control. That's the gap we fill.

IndicBridge
PKParth Khandagale· Introduction

Does a pivot help because it is related — or because it adds data?

RQ1 · family

Indo-Aryan vs Dravidian

Does Hindi help Marathi and Odia more than Kannada, under the same budget?

RQ2 · Odia

Which borrowed token?

Odia has no Whisper token. Bengali, Assamese or Hindi: does the choice matter?

RQ3 · scoring

Do the scoring rules change the answer?

How much do normalization choices move WER, and the ranking of methods?

So our main question: does a pivot language help because it is related to the target, or simply because it adds data?

Three supporting questions. One: Hindi is Indo-Aryan. Does it help the Indo-Aryan targets, Marathi and Odia, more than the Dravidian target Kannada?

Two: Odia has no token in Whisper, so we have to borrow one. Does it matter which?

Three: Indian scripts are easy to score wrongly. Do the scoring rules change the answer?

Gourab will now explain how we set up the experiment to answer these.

GDGourab Dash· Approach

One thing changes: the pivot.

25
training and evaluation runs
1
Apple M4 laptop, 16 GB
Pivot 2,000 steps · target 1,000 steps. Same data budget, optimiser, decoding and scoring for every run; only the first stage differs.

Thanks, Parth. Here is the whole design on one slide. Only one thing changes: the pivot.

We start from whisper-base. Path one: train on 45 hours of Hindi, the related pivot. Path two: 45 hours of English, same hours, same 2,000 steps, but unrelated to every target. That's our control. Path three: no pivot at all, which is direct training.

Then each model is trained on the target, Marathi, Odia or Kannada, 15 hours and 1,000 steps, and scored on two test sets, FLEURS and Kathbath, 600 clips each.

So if Hindi beats English, it can't be because of more data or an extra stage. Both pivots had exactly the same.

If family is what matters, Hindi should help Marathi and Odia more than Kannada.

Why these three targets? Because together they separate family from script.

Marathi is Hindi's close relative and even uses the same Devanagari script. Odia is in the same family but has its own script, and Whisper has no token for it. Kannada is from a different family altogether, Dravidian, with its own script.

So the prediction is clear: if language family drives the gain, Hindi should help Marathi and Odia more than Kannada. If it's mostly shared script, Marathi alone should stand out.

Why base? whisper-small trained at 1.35 clips/s here (~49 h for the grid); base at 4.54 (~15 h).

The data. For Hindi and the three targets we used IndicVoices, natural speech from real Indian speakers. Hindi: 19,127 clips from 1,474 speakers. English comes from LibriSpeech audiobooks. The test sets are FLEURS and Kathbath, which we never train on.

The model is whisper-base. We freeze its 74 million weights and train only small LoRA matrices on the attention layers: 1.18 million parameters, 1.6 percent of the model.

Why base and not small? We measured it: whisper-small would have needed about 49 hours for the full grid on our laptop; base needed about 15. Our question compares methods, so a smaller model answers it fairly. The absolute error rates are higher, and we say so.

Odia is the hardest case, and this slide shows why. Whisper's tokenizer has almost no Odia pieces, so it writes each letter as raw UTF-8 bytes. The grey chips are single bytes. Only the spaces, in purple, are real tokens.

This short sentence costs 134 tokens for 42 letters. On average Odia needs 3.09 tokens per letter; Hindi needs 1.29.

Whisper's decoder can only write about 448 tokens, so 23.1% of Odia test sentences are simply too long to ever be transcribed, by any model. We excluded them for every model and report the share.

And because there's no Odia token, we borrowed Bengali's, its closest relative, chosen before seeing any results.

IndicBridge
GDGourab Dash· Approach

Score Indian scripts carefully, or the numbers lie.

The trap
Sentenceनमस्ते आप कैसे हैं Our normalizerनमस्ते आप कैसे हैं Whisper'sनमस त आप क स ह

Whisper's normalizer deletes every vowel sign and splits words. We score with our own (NFC, punctuation and danda removed, vowel signs kept) and report Whisper's as a third column.

What we measure

WER = (S + D + I) / N
G(t) = WERdirect − WERpivot→t
Δ(t) = GHindi − GEnglish

Every gain gets a 95% interval from a paired bootstrap: 1,000 resamples of the test clips, both models scored on the same clips.

Scoring Indian languages has a trap. Take "namaste, aap kaise hain". Whisper's own normalizer deletes every vowel sign, the matras, and splits the words apart. That makes error rates look much better than they are.

So we wrote our own normalizer that keeps the vowel signs, and shared it across the team with a checksum so everyone scored identically. We still report Whisper's score as a third column, because the difference is itself a finding.

What we measure: WER, word error rate. The gain G: how many WER points a pivot saves over direct training. And Delta: the Hindi gain minus the English gain, which isolates the effect of relatedness.

Every number comes with a 95% confidence interval from a paired bootstrap.

IndicBridge
GDGourab Dash· Approach

What broke along the way, and the fix.

The Hindi pivot ran out of memory
Apple's GPU cached a new compute graph for every label length: 4.9 GB on top of the model.
pad labels to multiples of 64 (7 shapes), micro-batch 2 × 8, effective batch still 16
Default decoding broke Odia
A repetition penalty blocks Odia's repeating byte tokens; a 200-token cap cut sentences short.
plain greedy decoding, no penalties, a length cap per language
36–59 GB of audio per language
Too big to download whole; first-N sampling would pick one district.
seeded sampling across shards, 2–30 s clips, ≤50 clips per speaker
The offline model disagreed with PyTorch
MLX decoded with timestamps on; our adapters were trained without them. Some clips looped.
timestamps off (Kannada CER 35.6 → 24.4), loop fallback: within 2.5 WER of PyTorch

Running 25 experiments on one laptop meant solving real problems. Four of them.

One: the Hindi pivot crashed out of memory. Apple's GPU caches a compiled graph for every different label length. We padded labels to multiples of 64, so only seven shapes exist.

Two: the decoding settings from our plan broke Odia. A repetition penalty blocks exactly the byte tokens Odia repeats, so we switched to plain greedy decoding for every run.

Three: IndicVoices is up to 59 GB per language, so we sampled across the whole dataset with a fixed seed.

Four: our offline model didn't match PyTorch until we turned timestamps off, the way it was trained.

Now Divyansh will show what we found.

Thank you, Gourab. First, the overall picture: fine-tuning works.

Untrained, every language is above 100 percent error. After training, Hindi drops from 154.7 to 41.0 on FLEURS, and every trained model writes 100 percent in the correct script, up from between 0 and 7 percent.

The absolute numbers, 60 to 75 percent, are high because whisper-base is small. What matters is the comparison, and look at the purple numbers: Hindi-first is the best method in all six cells, for every target on both test sets.

But is that because Hindi is related, or just because it's extra data? That's the next slide.

IndicBridge
DMDivyansh Mahecha· Results

Hindi helps. English doesn't.

Hindi pivot, 45 hEnglish pivot, 45 h

WER points saved over direct training · dot: gain · line: 95% interval

This is our main result. Each dot is how many WER points a pivot saves over training on the target alone; the line is the 95% confidence interval. Right of zero means it helped.

The brown dots, Hindi, are to the right for every target: Marathi +3.1 and +3.5, Odia +3.1 and +1.9, Kannada +1.1 and +0.8.

The blue dots, English, sit on zero. Same 45 hours, same 2,000 steps, and no significant gain anywhere. For Kannada on FLEURS it even hurts, −1.3.

So the gain is not about data quantity or the extra training stage. Equal English data adds nothing.

Positive for all three, Dravidian Kannada included. A bigger effect for the Indo-Aryan targets shows only once: Marathi vs Kannada on Kathbath, +2.7 [1.0, 4.8].

Hindi pivot on Kannada audio, before any Kannada training
Said (Kannada script)ಸಹ ಕುಸ್ತಿಪಟುಗಳು ಸಹ ಲೂನಾ ಅವರಿಗೆ ಗೌರವ ಸಲ್ಲಿಸಿದರು.
Written (Devanagari)सहाकुस्ती पटुगलु सहा लूना वरेगे दौरवा सलीसी दरू

The sounds carry over across families; only the script is wrong. On Marathi, which shares the script, CER already falls from 124.7 to 40.8.

Now RQ1: is it the language family? Here is Delta, the Hindi gain minus the English gain. It is positive for all three targets on both test sets, including Kannada, which is Dravidian.

If family were everything, Kannada should get nothing. It doesn't: Hindi beats English for Kannada by +2.5 and +1.9. A bigger Indo-Aryan effect appears only once, Marathi versus Kannada on Kathbath, and Marathi also shares Hindi's script, so we can't separate script from family there.

The right side shows why. The Hindi model, before any Kannada training, hears Kannada and writes it phonetically in Devanagari: "saha kusti patugalu…". The sounds transfer; only the script is wrong.

So our answer: relatedness, but regional. Shared Indian sounds help even across families. Over to Kaushal.

Thanks, Divyansh. RQ2: Odia has no token, so which one should we borrow?

Untrained, it doesn't matter, because all three give zero percent Odia script. After training, all three give 100 percent, and the error rates are within about one point: Bengali 74.5, Assamese 74.9, Hindi 73.8 on FLEURS.

None of the differences is statistically reliable, and the genealogically closest languages, Bengali and Assamese, don't win.

So for Odia, the token is not the problem. The real ceiling is the tokenizer: 23.1 percent of Odia sentences are too long for Whisper to ever write.

Hindi-first stays best under all three rules.

fp16: 144 MB, 17–31× faster than real time

Within 2.5 WER of PyTorch on the same clips. 4-bit is 3.4× smaller (42 MB) but 6–13 WER worse, and Kannada CER jumps from 17.0 to 72.1. We ship fp16.

Open the live demo →

RQ3, scoring. If you score with Whisper's own normalizer, Marathi WER falls from 60.3 to 30.5, roughly half, because it deletes vowel signs. A paper using it would report numbers that look far better than they are. The good news: Hindi-first stays best under all three rules.

Deployment: we converted the models to Apple's MLX. The fp16 model is 144 MB and runs 17 to 31 times faster than real time on this laptop, fully offline. 4-bit is smaller but too lossy; it breaks Kannada.

KBKaushal BC· Results & close

What we can't claim yet, and what's next.

Limitations

· One training seed per run: intervals cover test sampling, not retraining.

· whisper-base only; absolute WER is high.

· The English stage moved the model less (loss 0.49 → 0.08, update norm 29.6 vs 36.2) and comes from audiobooks.

· Marathi shares Hindi's script, so script and family are entangled.

· Native-speaker error analysis not completed.

Future scope

· A Dravidian pivot (Tamil, Telugu) to test transfer the other way.

· Marathi → Odia and Kannada → Odia pivots.

· Several seeds; whisper-small and larger.

· Targets that separate script from family.

· A tokenizer that doesn't split Odia letters into bytes.

We want to be clear about the limits. One training seed per configuration, so our intervals cover the test sample, not retraining. whisper-base only.

The English control isn't perfect: Whisper already knows English, so that stage changed the model less, and LibriSpeech is audiobooks. And Marathi shares Hindi's script, so for Marathi, script and family are tangled together.

Next steps: a Dravidian pivot like Tamil or Telugu, to test transfer the other way; more seeds and bigger models; and a tokenizer that can actually write Odia.

KBKaushal BC· Results & close

Three things to remember.

1

It is not data quantity.

The same 45 hours of English added nothing; Hindi helped every target.

2

Relatedness, but regional.

Hindi helps even Dravidian Kannada; a family-only effect is not established.

3

For Odia, the tokenizer is the ceiling.

The borrowed token barely matters; 23% of sentences can't be written at all.

Thank you. Questions?

To wrap up, three things to remember.

One: the benefit of a pivot is not just data. Same hours of English, nothing.

Two: it's relatedness, but regional. Hindi helps even Kannada, from a different family, so choose pivots by shared sounds and region, not family alone.

Three: for Odia, the bottleneck is the tokenizer, not the language token.

Everything you saw runs on this laptop, offline, and every number comes from our results files. Thank you. We're happy to take questions.
